questions.q: What are the criteria necessary for an effective and efficient network?
questions.theory:
Network types by size:
• PAN — few meters. Ex: Bluetooth between phone and earbuds
• LAN — one building/campus. Ex: office computers linked to one printer
• MAN — one city, links multiple LANs. Ex: cable TV network across a city
• WAN — country/global. Ex: the Internet itself
Topologies (physical layout of wires/devices):
• Bus — all devices share one single central cable. Ex: old Ethernet coax networks
• Star — all devices connect to one central hub/switch. Ex: most modern office LANs
• Ring — each device connects to exactly 2 neighbours, forming a loop. Ex: old Token Ring networks
• Mesh — every device connects to every other device directly. Ex: military/defence networks needing high reliability
• Tree — star networks linked together in a hierarchy. Ex: large campus network with multiple buildings
• Hybrid — combination of 2+ topologies. Ex: a company using star LANs in each branch, connected via a bus backbone
Key devices:
• Router — connects two different networks. Ex: connects your home network to the ISP's network
• Switch — connects multiple devices within one LAN. Ex: connects all PCs in one office room
• Modem — converts digital signal↔analog signal. Ex: connects a home PC to a telephone/cable line
• Gateway — connects networks using different protocols. Ex: connects a company's internal network to the internet
Key protocols:
• TCP/IP — core rule-set of the internet. Ex: every website you visit uses it
• HTTP/HTTPS — transfers web pages. Ex: browser loading a website
• FTP — transfers files between computers. Ex: uploading a file to a web server
• DNS — converts domain name to IP address. Ex: turns "google.com" into its numeric IP
• DHCP — auto-assigns IP addresses to devices. Ex: your phone gets an IP automatically on joining WiFi
OSI Model (7 layers, top→bottom) — each with what it does + example:
1. Application — interacts with the user/software. Ex: browser, email client
2. Presentation — formats/encrypts/compresses data. Ex: converting data to JPEG or encrypting with SSL
3. Session — opens/manages/closes a connection session. Ex: keeping a video call connected
4. Transport — reliable end-to-end delivery. Ex: TCP breaking a file into segments
5. Network — routing/addressing across networks. Ex: IP deciding the path a packet takes
6. Data Link — node-to-node delivery on the same network. Ex: MAC addressing, Ethernet frames
7. Physical — actual transmission of raw bits. Ex: cables, radio signals, voltage levels
